title: Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism

blocks.text: Theme 3.1 · Investment, inclusion and sustainability · Focus area 14
Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism
Climate is already costing the province sites, routes and revenue, while the local tourism bodies that would manage the response depend on municipal funding that MFMA Circular No. 131 has disrupted.

Growth to 2035 rests on sites and routes that weather can close, and the losses already fall on the flagship sites (section 2.4). Each district carries its own climate risk, from water security on the Garden Route to extreme summer heat in the Central Karoo (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p43; Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p86). Water scarcity acts as a hard ceiling on visitor load in high-growth nodes such as the Garden Route (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p38). A risk spread across every district needs an owner in each. The risk weighs most where tourism weighs most. In 2023 tourist spend equalled 15.6% to 16.8% of GDPR in the Garden Route, Overberg, West Coast and Central Karoo, against 6.7% in the Metro (Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Garden Route, p151; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Overberg, p119; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, West Coast, p131; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Central Karoo, p111; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Cape Metro, p72).

Yet the bodies that should manage the response locally are the weakest link. The Department of Economic Development rates Western Cape and Cape Town funding for destination management and marketing materially below peer destinations. It also finds that most local tourism organisations (LTOs) cannot sustain operations without municipal funding, which MFMA Circular No. 131 has disrupted (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p25). A body unsure of next year's budget cannot plan for a flood or a fire season.

blocks.message: Climate losses are dated and site-specific, and the bodies that manage destinations locally have no stable funding.

blocks.text: The evidence is dated and site-specific, but it does not add up to a provincial picture. No source puts a provincial figure on tourism revenue at risk from weather or water [provincial estimate of tourism revenue at risk: none in hand]. None counts the LTOs or their grant funding [number of Western Cape LTOs and their municipal funding before and after Circular 131: DEDAT to supply]. The LTO funding finding rests on two organisations, the Department of Economic Development and the West Coast District Municipality (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p25, p39).

The response exists in pieces. Mossel Bay's membership inspections check water-wise and green practices, the only working sustainability standard on record (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p21). CapeNature is reassessing asset formats and siting to cut losses from flooding, fire and extreme weather (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p43). What is missing is a provincial record of losses and a stable owner for local destination management.

Wesgro should treat climate as a destination-management risk it records and plans around, and press for stable funding of the local bodies that do the work. In 2027 and 2028 DEDAT and Wesgro's Research unit build a climate and weather risk register for sites and routes, starting with the dated losses (section 4.3). They also design an LTO funding model that answers Circular 131 and tests the Blueprint's district model (focus area 16). Wesgro routes itineraries around Meiringspoort while it is closed. From 2029 funding agreements with a development mandate are signed, and routing around closures draws on the register. The quality charter carries sustainability checks on the Mossel Bay model (focus area 11). From 2029 climate risk and LTO funding also enter municipal IDPs, with reporting. The route exists: the Provincial Treasury writes its district reviews to inform IDPs and budgets, and they already carry environmental risk data (Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Cape Metro, p4 to p5).

The register comes first, because routing, funding and capital choices all depend on knowing which sites close and how often. Three districts then have positions to build on: the Cape Winelands as a climate-smart wine region, the Overberg as a nature-positive test bed and the Garden Route as a case for resilience investment (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p45, p49, p43).

blocks.text: The register turns scattered losses into decisions. Some losses already carry a figure: weather cancellations cost Robben Island roughly R16m a year, and the Meiringspoort rebuild costs R421m (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p33; SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p24). Once losses are dated and costed by site, Wesgro can route itineraries around a closure and operators can weigh resilience spending against the loss it avoids. Stable funding works on the other half. An LTO with a multi-year agreement and a development mandate can plan for a fire season, not only the next campaign.

The evidence diagnoses this risk more than it prescribes for it. No comparator carries a climate-adaptation or local funding lever, so the precedents are partial. Kenya finances conservation from tourism, a self-financing system that supports conservation and sustains tourism demand (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p33). Valencia runs its SICTED quality system with environmental compliance frameworks, and counts a stronger reputation for quality and sustainability among the results (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p47). Mossel Bay's inspections show the same checks can work at town scale. The condition is national. Until the effect of Circular 131 is resolved, the funding agreements the plan needs rest on uncertain ground.

**Initiative I13**, climate resilience and destination management, including LTO funding (section 4.3). **Indicators** T2-18 LTOs with a funding agreement and T2-19 weather losses at flagship sites at outcome level (section 5.2).
